Originally the Iran and Libya Sanctions Act. It pioneered secondary sanctions by penalizing foreign companies, not just U.S. ones, that invest in Iran's energy sector.

::: {.official-links}
**Read the law** (official GovInfo text)

[Enacted text: Pub. L. 104-172](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/104/public/172){.btn-official} [Current U.S. Code: 50 U.S.C. 1701 note](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/1701?link-type=html){.btn-official}
:::

## Key provisions

- Requires the President to impose a menu of sanctions on firms making significant investments in Iranian petroleum development.
- Libya was removed in 2006.
- Expanded in 2010 by the Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability, and Divestment Act to cover refined petroleum and financial institutions, and again in 2012.
- Includes presidential waiver authority, which has been the main point of leverage in negotiations.

## Why it matters

It established the model of extraterritorial sanctions later applied to Russia and others in [CAATSA](caatsa-2017.qmd). Whether its sanctions could be waived was the statutory question behind the 2015 nuclear deal and the [Iran Nuclear Review Act](inara-2015.qmd).

## Current status

In force through December 31, 2026 under the Iran Sanctions Extension Act (Pub. L. 114-277). The sunset is imminent as of this wiki's last review. Check whether it has been extended.
